## The brief is deliberately too large

```{=html}
<div class="stage opening-stage">
  <div>
    <div class="eyebrow">THE STARTING POINT</div>
    <p class="big-claim">Choose work that one agent cannot hold in its head.</p>
    <div class="metric-line"><b>Many</b><span>subsystems and platforms</span></div>
    <div class="metric-line"><b>Many</b><span>workers in parallel</span></div>
    <div class="metric-line"><b>One</b><span>coherent product</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="system-map" aria-label="A large product divided into architectural regions">
    <div class="map-node domain"><b>Domain</b><span>model · rules</span></div>
    <div class="map-node engine"><b>Engine</b><span>commands · state</span></div>
    <div class="map-node io"><b>Data</b><span>I/O · protocols</span></div>
    <div class="map-node ui"><b>Interface</b><span>desktop · web</span></div>
    <div class="map-node tools"><b>Automation</b><span>CLI · agents</span></div>
    <div class="map-node proof"><b>Evidence</b><span>tests · scorecards</span></div>
    <div class="map-center"><b>REPOSITORY</b><span>the shared model of reality</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The interesting swarm problems are too large for one worker to understand at once.  They cross subsystems, platforms, tools, and definitions of done.

The trick is not to give every agent more context.  The trick is to arrange the repository so that each agent needs less context, while the finished pieces still compose into one product.

This is an architectural problem before it is a prompting problem.
:::

## `AGENTS.md` is the control plane

```{=html}
<div class="stage document-stage">
  <div class="artifact paper">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>AGENTS.md</span><span>read first</span></div>
    <h3>One shared operating manual</h3>
    <div class="rule"><b>Orient</b><span>Architecture, roadmap, gaps, scorecard</span></div>
    <div class="rule"><b>Choose</b><span>Highest-ranked work that nobody owns</span></div>
    <div class="rule"><b>Build</b><span>One command, one module, one testable slice</span></div>
    <div class="rule"><b>Finish</b><span>Run the gates and leave a terse dev log</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="side-copy">
    <p class="big-claim compact">The prompt is part of the codebase.</p>
    <p>Every worker starts with the same map, rules, and definition of done.</p>
    <p class="accent-note">Less private context.  Fewer invented conventions.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The first artifact is the operating manual.  `AGENTS.md` is not a welcome note.  It records how work is chosen, where code belongs, which files are shared, how changes are validated, and what a clean handoff looks like.

That moves maintainer judgment out of private conversations and into versioned project state.  Every worker begins with the same rules, and the rules evolve with the software.

Specific instructions beat vague encouragement.  “Dependencies point down” and “new behavior gets a new module” are useful.  “Write good code” is not.
:::

## Architecture is a map of safe ownership

```{=html}
<div class="architecture-stage">
  <div class="layer-stack">
    <div class="layer l6"><b>L6</b><span>interfaces · automation</span></div>
    <div class="layer l5"><b>L5</b><span>application services · command registry</span></div>
    <div class="layer l4"><b>L4</b><span>adapters · storage · protocols</span></div>
    <div class="layer l3"><b>L3</b><span>compute · scheduling · composition</span></div>
    <div class="layer l2"><b>L2</b><span>domain algorithms</span></div>
    <div class="layer l1"><b>L1</b><span>domain model</span></div>
    <div class="layer l0"><b>L0</b><span>types · geometry · codecs</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="side-copy architecture-copy">
    <div class="eyebrow">ARTIFACT · architecture.md</div>
    <p class="big-claim compact">Dependencies may only point downward.</p>
    <p><code>check-layers</code> enforces the rule.  The diagram is not a suggestion.</p>
    <p class="accent-note">A worker can own one region without learning the entire system.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Parallel work needs boundaries that a machine can enforce.  The architecture document describes layers, allowed dependencies, public seams, and ownership zones.

A layer checker turns the diagram into a rule.  A worker changing storage cannot quietly reach into the interface.  A worker adding a command cannot bypass the domain model.

The architecture therefore does two jobs.  It keeps the software clean, and it reduces the amount of context needed to make a safe change.
:::

## The product surface is a contract

```{=html}
<div class="stage menu-stage">
  <div class="artifact code-paper">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>surface_catalog.toml</span><span>versioned</span></div>
    <div class="menu-row"><span>Workspace</span><b>Open</b><code>workspace.open</code></div>
    <div class="menu-row"><span>Document</span><b>Transform</b><code>document.transform</code></div>
    <div class="menu-row"><span>Data</span><b>Import</b><code>data.import</code></div>
    <div class="menu-row"><span>Output</span><b>Export</b><code>output.export</code></div>
  </div>
  <div class="menu-result">
    <div class="ring"><span>KNOWN</span><small>product surface</small></div>
    <p>Matching command found: enabled.<br>Missing implementation: visible, but incomplete.</p>
    <p class="accent-note">Ambition becomes a measurable backlog.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
A swarm needs a finite description of the product it is trying to build.  The surface catalog records every user-visible capability with a stable identifier.

Those identifiers join interface, engine, automation, documentation, and tracking.  When an implementation registers the identifier, every client can discover it.  When it is missing, the gap remains visible.

The catalog prevents a common failure mode: lots of locally impressive work with no reliable picture of whether the product is becoming complete.
:::

## Everything becomes one command

```{=html}
<div class="command-stage">
  <div class="artifact command-spec">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>CommandSpec</span><span>the application seam</span></div>
    <pre><code>id        "document.transform"
label     "Transform…"
params    { mode, amount }
enabled   has_active_document
run       transform_document
undo      restore_snapshot</code></pre>
  </div>
  <div class="clients">
    <div><b>Desktop</b><span>menu or gesture</span></div>
    <div><b>CLI</b><span>headless run</span></div>
    <div><b>Agent</b><span>structured tool</span></div>
    <div><b>Replay</b><span>recorded action</span></div>
  </div>
  <p class="command-caption">Four clients.  One behavior.  One undo boundary.</p>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The command registry is the central seam.  A command carries its stable ID, parameters, precondition, implementation, result, and undo behavior.

Every client converges on that registry.  The interface does not contain a second implementation.  The automation layer does not invent another API.  Recorded actions do not bypass validation.

This makes functionality composable.  It also gives agents a small, typed place to discover and extend behavior.
:::

## The backlog is executable

```{=html}
<div class="tracking-stage">
  <div class="tracking-doc road"><span>ROADMAP.md</span><b>What matters now?</b><small>stage · milestones · honest readiness</small></div>
  <div class="tracking-doc gaps"><span>docs/gaps.md</span><b>What should a worker pick?</b><small>ranked by user impact and dependency</small></div>
  <div class="tracking-doc score"><span>scorecard/*.toml</span><b>What counts as done?</b><small>status · issue · evidence · budget</small></div>
  <div class="tracking-doc report"><span>docs/scorecard.md</span><b>Does the report match reality?</b><small>generated · checked in CI</small></div>
</div>
<p class="tracking-caption">Strategy becomes a queue.  The queue becomes evidence.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
The work queue belongs in the repository too.  The roadmap says where the product is going.  The gaps document ranks missing behavior.  Machine-readable scorecards attach status, evidence, and budgets to individual capabilities.

A worker can choose useful work without a meeting.  More importantly, the same worker updates the evidence when the change lands.  CI regenerates reports and rejects stale claims.

This keeps the swarm aimed at user value rather than whatever task happens to be easiest to prompt.
:::

## The repository runs the swarm

```{=html}
<div class="swarm-stage">
  <div class="agent-field" aria-label="Several independent agents working around a shared repository">
    <span class="agent a1">A</span><span class="agent a2">A</span><span class="agent a3">A</span><span class="agent a4">A</span>
    <span class="agent a5">A</span><span class="agent a6">A</span><span class="agent a7">A</span><span class="agent a8">A</span>
    <div class="repo-core"><span class="repo-glyph">{ }</span><b>REPO</b><small>rules · queue · evidence</small></div>
  </div>
  <div class="swarm-rules">
    <div><b>Isolated workspaces</b><span>No shared build-state queue</span></div>
    <div><b>Explicit file ownership</b><span>Small edits to shared registries</span></div>
    <div><b>Additive modules</b><span>Parallel changes rarely collide</span></div>
    <div><b>Green handoffs</b><span>The next worker starts from a stable tree</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
There is no magical conductor in the middle.  The repository coordinates the swarm.

Workers use isolated workspaces, claim narrow file sets, add behavior in new modules, and keep edits to shared registries small.  The shared artifacts tell each worker what matters and what finished means.

This looks more like a distributed system than a group chat.  Workers do not need identical knowledge.  They need stable contracts, low-conflict write paths, and a reliable shared state.
:::

## Vertical slices keep merges boring

```{=html}
<div class="slice-stage">
  <div class="slice-list">
    <div><i>01</i><b>Choose one visible gap</b><span>One outcome, not a subsystem rewrite</span></div>
    <div><i>02</i><b>Add one command module</b><span><code>transform_command.rs</code></span></div>
    <div><i>03</i><b>Reuse the lower layer</b><span><code>domain::transform</code></span></div>
    <div><i>04</i><b>Prove failure and success</b><span>bad input · output · undo</span></div>
    <div><i>05</i><b>Raise the evidence</b><span>catalog · scorecard · dev log</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="slice-proof artifact">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>change set</span><span>small enough to review</span></div>
    <div class="proof-line add"><b>+</b><span>src/commands/transform.rs</span></div>
    <div class="proof-line add"><b>+</b><span>tests/transform_fixture.rs</span></div>
    <div class="proof-line edit"><b>±</b><span>src/commands/registry.rs</span></div>
    <div class="proof-line edit"><b>±</b><span>scorecard/capabilities.toml</span></div>
    <div class="proof-result"><span>tests</span><b>PASS</b><span>layers</span><b>PASS</b><span>evidence</span><b>UPDATED</b></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The unit of parallel work is a vertical slice, not a broad layer.  A useful slice starts with one visible gap, adds one command, reuses or extends a lower-level capability, proves success and failure, and updates the evidence.

That shape is easy to review and easy to merge.  It avoids the swarm failure where one worker builds a framework, another builds an interface, and neither quite matches the other.

Most files in the change are new.  Shared registries receive only the smallest possible edit.
:::

## Agents can operate the product

```{=html}
<div class="operate-stage">
  <div class="operate-code"><div class="artifact-bar"><span>agent control protocol</span><span>same command IDs</span></div><pre><code>command_list  { filter }
command_run   { id, params }
state_inspect { selection, history }
render_preview{ max_size }
ui_screenshot { live_window }</code></pre></div>
  <div class="observe-loop">
    <div><b>Inspect</b><span>state, commands, preconditions</span></div>
    <div><b>Act</b><span>the same application path as the UI</span></div>
    <div><b>See</b><span>bounded output or full screenshot</span></div>
    <div><b>Correct</b><span>use the returned error, not a guess</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="operate-caption">A bug report can become a runnable script.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Agents should be able to operate the software, not merely edit source and hope.  A small control protocol exposes the command catalog, preconditions, state, bounded previews, and interface screenshots.

The tools use the same command path as the human interface.  They do not create a privileged second application hidden behind the first.

This closes the loop: inspect, act, see, correct.  It also makes bug reports executable.  A reproduction can be a short command sequence rather than a paragraph about where somebody clicked.
:::

## Why Rust fits the framework

```{=html}
<div class="rust-stage">
  <div class="rust-word">Rust</div>
  <div class="rust-reasons">
    <div><b>One language</b><span>domain, native UI, CLI, automation, web build</span></div>
    <div><b>Explicit seams</b><span>types make architectural boundaries harder to blur</span></div>
    <div><b>Local reasoning</b><span>ownership exposes sharing and mutation</span></div>
    <div><b>Native speed</b><span>parallel CPU work and portable GPU compute</span></div>
    <div><b>Portable core</b><span>desktop platforms and WebAssembly</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The framework does not require Rust, but Rust reinforces its ideas unusually well.

Types make command and layer seams explicit.  Ownership makes sharing and mutation visible.  Errors are values rather than hidden control flow.  The domain, native interface, command-line tools, automation server, and browser build can live in one language and one workspace.

Rust does not make correctness automatic.  It does make many accidental forms of architectural drift harder to introduce across agent boundaries.
:::

## Tests and measures, not trust

```{=html}
<div class="qm-stage">
  <div class="qm-panel">
    <div class="eyebrow">TESTS · DOES IT BEHAVE?</div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Unit + property</b><span>every crate; generated inputs for the tricky data structures</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Round trips</b><span>read, write, compare byte for byte</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Hostile input</b><span>truncate at every offset; fuzz the parsers in CI</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Real files</b><span>pinned, checksum-verified corpora with pass floors</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Render oracle</b><span>compare output with the file's own embedded preview</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Agent tasks</b><span>realistic edits through the control API, checked by screenshot</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="qm-panel measures">
    <div class="eyebrow">MEASURES · HOW GOOD IS IT?</div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Perf budgets</b><span>named scenarios with targets; regressions fail</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Size gate</b><span>the web build must stay under its limit</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Coverage floor</b><span>the count of live commands can't go down</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Scorecard</b><span>generated from evidence; CI fails if it's stale</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="qm-gates">Every change also passes <b>format</b> · <b>lint</b> · <b>layers</b> · <b>cross-target builds</b></p>
```

::: {.notes}
The swarm expects workers to make mistakes, so quality has to be checked by machines, not assumed.  There are two kinds of check.

Tests answer "does it behave?".  Every crate has unit tests, with property tests generating inputs for the trickiest data structures.  File formats get byte-exact round trips, and hostile input: files truncated at every offset, plus fuzz targets for the parsers that run in CI.  Real-world files live in pinned, checksum-verified corpora, and the pass counts have floors that can't drop.  A render oracle compares the compositor's output with the image the file itself embeds.  And a set of realistic agent tasks drives the app through the control API and checks the result by screenshot.

Measures answer "how good is it?".  Performance scenarios each have a budget; anything not yet met is tracked, and regressions fail.  The web build has a size gate.  The count of live menu commands has a floor.  The scorecard is generated from all of this, and CI fails if the committed copy is stale.

Underneath, every change passes formatting, lint with warnings as errors, the layer checker, and the cross-target builds.  Workers run the narrow checks while they iterate, and the full relevant set before they hand off.
:::

## Fast does not mean finished

```{=html}
<div class="honesty-stage">
  <div class="maturity-board artifact">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>capability scorecard</span><span>evidence, not optimism</span></div>
    <div class="maturity-row"><span>Surface</span><div><i style="width: 94%"></i></div><b>known</b></div>
    <div class="maturity-row"><span>Behavior</span><div><i style="width: 68%"></i></div><b>tested</b></div>
    <div class="maturity-row"><span>Edge cases</span><div><i style="width: 43%"></i></div><b>partial</b></div>
    <div class="maturity-row"><span>Performance</span><div><i style="width: 31%"></i></div><b>measured</b></div>
    <div class="maturity-row"><span>Readiness</span><div><i style="width: 22%"></i></div><b>honest</b></div>
  </div>
  <div class="honesty-copy">
    <div class="eyebrow">BREADTH ≠ DEPTH</div>
    <p class="big-claim compact">A capability can exist without being mature.</p>
    <div class="paired-stat"><b>Surface</b><span>Can it be reached?<br><small>catalog + command</small></span></div>
    <div class="paired-stat warning"><b>Depth</b><span>Can it survive reality?<br><small>fixtures + budgets + edge cases</small></span></div>
    <p>Do not let a busy swarm manufacture confidence faster than software.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Swarming can produce astonishing breadth quickly.  That makes honest maturity tracking essential.

The scorecard separates existence from depth.  A command may be wired and reachable while its edge cases, performance budgets, platform coverage, or recovery paths remain incomplete.

That is useful information, not an embarrassment.  It prevents feature counts from being mistaken for readiness and gives the next wave of workers something concrete to improve.
:::

## Field notes from two swarms

```{=html}
<div class="fn-divider">
  <div class="eyebrow">APPENDIX · FOR REVIEW</div>
  <p class="big-claim">What running real swarms actually taught me.</p>
```

## Two swarms, one week

```{=html}
<div class="fn-two">
  <div class="fn-swarm a">
    <div class="eyebrow">SWARM A · STARTED 13 OCT</div>
    <p class="fn-what">Rewrite a large desktop application, with the original as the golden reference.</p>
    <div class="fn-stats">
      <div><b>~940</b><span>commits</span></div>
      <div><b>217</b><span>merges</span></div>
      <div><b>43</b><span>owner directions</span></div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="fn-link">
    <div class="fn-arrow right"><span>tracking data</span></div>
    <div class="fn-arrow left"><span>process fixes</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="fn-swarm b">
    <div class="eyebrow">SWARM B · STARTED 17 OCT</div>
    <p class="fn-what">Build a timeline inspector that shows what Swarm A is doing.</p>
    <div class="fn-stats">
      <div><b>~420</b><span>commits</span></div>
      <div><b>3</b><span>days</span></div>
      <div><b>38</b><span>owner directions</span></div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="fn-caption">One swarm built the product.  The other built the instrument to watch it.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Two swarms, running side by side for about a week.

Swarm A is a rewrite of a large desktop application, using the original product as the golden reference.  Swarm B is a timeline inspector: it reads Swarm A's tracking data and shows which agent worked on what, and when.

They ended up improving each other.  Swarm A's tracking data feeds Swarm B, and fixes to the process found while building Swarm B flowed back into Swarm A.

Counts are from the repositories on 19 October and are approximate.
:::

## The owner keeps a ledger

```{=html}
<div class="stage document-stage">
  <div class="artifact paper fn-ledger">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>docs/owner-directions.md</span><span>read with AGENTS.md</span></div>
    <div class="fn-line"><i>10-14</i><span>Real applications drive the work, not toy demos.</span></div>
    <div class="fn-line"><i>10-15</i><span>The original is the golden reference.  Do what it does.</span></div>
    <div class="fn-line"><i>10-15</i><span>When something fails, the UI must say so.</span></div>
    <div class="fn-line"><i>10-17</i><span>The coordinator claims its own work, too.</span></div>
    <div class="fn-line"><i>10-18</i><span>Capacity is measured, not guessed.</span></div>
    <div class="fn-line fade"><i>…</i><span>a revision table at the bottom</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="side-copy">
    <p class="big-claim compact">One line per direction.  Dated.  Newest wins.</p>
    <p>When it disagrees with <code>AGENTS.md</code>, the ledger wins and <code>AGENTS.md</code> is updated to match.</p>
    <p class="accent-note">Agents add a line whenever I decide something.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The most useful single file turned out to be a ledger of my decisions.  One line per direction, each dated, newest decisions winning.

Agents read it alongside AGENTS.md.  If the two disagree, the more recent direction wins and AGENTS.md gets fixed.  There's a small revision table at the bottom, so you can see how the direction changed over time.

The important habit is that the agents maintain it.  When I make a call in a conversation, it becomes a line in the file, so the next worker, who never saw that conversation, still knows.
:::

## Steer with decisions, not prompts

```{=html}
<div class="fn-flow">
  <div class="fn-step"><i>01</i><b>The swarm writes a plan</b><span>with numbered recommendations and open questions</span></div>
  <div class="fn-step"><i>02</i><b>I answer the questions</b><span>“all eight recommendations approved”</span></div>
  <div class="fn-step"><i>03</i><b>Answers become directions</b><span>one dated line each, in the ledger</span></div>
  <div class="fn-step"><i>04</i><b>The plan becomes tickets</b><span>phases filed, in whatever order makes sense</span></div>
</div>
<p class="fn-caption">My job became answering good questions, not writing prompts.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Big pieces of work started as a plan written by the swarm, not by me.  Each plan ended with numbered recommendations and a short list of questions only the owner could answer.

I answered them, sometimes in a sentence: all eight recommendations approved.  The answers went straight into the ledger, and the plan was split into tickets.

That changed what my day looked like.  Less prompting, more product management: deciding, approving, and setting the quality bar.
:::

## A golden reference beats a spec

```{=html}
<div class="fn-ref">
  <div class="fn-ref-claim">
    <div class="eyebrow">THE RULE</div>
    <p class="big-claim">Do what the original does, unless there is a reason not to.</p>
    <p class="fn-small">Accessibility is a reason.  Taste is not.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="fn-ref-rules">
    <div><b>Match, don't exceed</b><span>a menu item the original never enables stays disabled</span></div>
    <div><b>Use it as an oracle</b><span>compare results event by event through its own API</span></div>
    <div><b>Read it for gotchas</b><span>its source knows how real apps misbehave</span></div>
    <div><b>Never modify it</b><span>study it, run it, never change it</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
A spec is never complete, and agents fill the gaps with their own ideas.  A working product to copy is much better.

The rule was simple: do what the original does, unless there's a real reason not to.  Accessibility was a good reason; we kept a few contrast fixes.  Personal taste was not.

Match it, rather than going beyond it: if the original never enables a menu item, ours doesn't either.  Use the original's own scripting API as an oracle to compare results event by event.  Read its source for the ways real applications misuse the API.  And never, ever modify the reference install.
:::

## Toy targets mislead

```{=html}
<div class="fn-vs">
  <div class="fn-card bad">
    <div class="eyebrow">THE TOY</div>
    <b>One tiny demo app</b>
    <ul>
      <li>Every feature worked on it</li>
      <li>Tests run 20 times over</li>
      <li>The code bent around its quirks</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
  <div class="fn-vs-mark">→</div>
  <div class="fn-card good">
    <div class="eyebrow">THE REAL WORLD</div>
    <b>Public sample suites</b>
    <ul>
      <li>Dozens of real applications</li>
      <li>Run once, twice to confirm a fix</li>
      <li>Failures point at real gaps</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="fn-caption">The early focus on the toy was too invasive.  Real workloads drive the work.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Early on the swarm leaned hard on one tiny demo application.  Everything worked on it, tests were run over and over, and the code started bending around that one app's quirks.

I redirected the work to public sample suites: dozens of real applications.  Repeated runs stopped too; once, then twice to confirm a fix, and leave the rest to CI.

The toy is still useful for testing a mechanism.  It just isn't representative, and a swarm will happily optimize for whatever target you hand it.
:::

## How work moves through the swarm

```{=html}
<div class="fn-pipe">
  <div class="fn-pipe-row">
    <div class="fn-node"><b>Issue</b><span>ranked in the tracker</span></div>
    <div class="fn-node claim"><b>Claim</b><span>label + comment</span></div>
    <div class="fn-node"><b>Worktree</b><span>one per worker</span></div>
    <div class="fn-node"><b>MR</b><span>with a Progress section</span></div>
    <div class="fn-node gate"><b>Local gate</b><span>the full check, on real hardware</span></div>
    <div class="fn-node merge"><b>Merge</b><span>by the coordinator</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="fn-roles">
    <div><b>Workers</b><span>claim an issue, build it in their own worktree, open an MR, clean up when it closes</span></div>
    <div><b>Coordinator</b><span>starts workers, merges on a green local gate, watches main, stops merging while it's red</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The process settled into a simple pipeline.  Issues are ranked in the tracker.  A worker claims one by adding a label and a comment, builds it in its own worktree, and opens a merge request.

The coordinator merges on a green local gate, run on real hardware, rather than waiting for a CI pipeline.  It then watches main's pipeline and stops merging while it's red.

One lesson here: the coordinator has to claim its own work too, however small.  Otherwise a worker picks up the same issue and you get duplicates.
:::

## Shared files are merge magnets

```{=html}
<div class="fn-magnet">
  <div class="fn-files">
    <div class="eyebrow">WORKERS DON'T EDIT</div>
    <div class="fn-file struck">ROADMAP.md</div>
    <div class="fn-file struck">docs/roadmap.md</div>
    <div class="fn-file struck">docs/gaps.md</div>
  </div>
  <div class="fn-instead">
    <div class="fn-hop"><b>Each MR</b><span>carries a Progress note: measured numbers, what moved, what's open</span></div>
    <div class="fn-hop"><b>The coordinator</b><span>updates the summaries once per batch</span></div>
    <div class="fn-hop"><b>The tracker</b><span>stays the board: claims need live state across two machines</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Every worker wanted to update the roadmap and the gaps list when it finished something.  With several workers, those files became merge conflicts waiting to happen.

So workers stopped editing them.  Each merge request carries a short Progress section instead, with the measured numbers and what's still open.  The coordinator rolls those up into the summaries once per batch.

For the same reason the issue tracker stayed the board, rather than a Kanban folder in the repository.  With a Mac and a desktop PC both taking work, claims need shared live state.
:::

## Make the swarm observable

```{=html}
<div class="fn-observe">
  <div class="artifact fn-jsonl">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>tracking/&lt;instance&gt;/work.jsonl</span><span>tracking branch</span></div>
<pre><code>{"event":"session.start","role":"worker","name":"spruce"}
{"event":"claim","issue":80,"mr":87}
{"event":"work","issue":80}
{"event":"submit","issue":80,"mr":87}
{"event":"stop","issue":80,"reason":"done"}
{"event":"session.stop"}</code></pre>
  </div>
  <div class="fn-verbs">
    <div class="eyebrow">EVERY AGENT LOGS</div>
    <div class="fn-chips"><span>session</span><span>claim</span><span>work</span><span>submit</span><span>stop</span><span>release</span><span class="c">merge</span><span class="c">send-back</span></div>
    <p>One small JSON line per event, on a branch of its own.</p>
    <p class="accent-note">It must stay small and never hold the swarm back.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Once there were several agents, I couldn't tell what was going on by reading chat.  So every agent, workers and coordinator, logs its sessions and its work on issues to a tracking branch: one small JSON line per event.

Workers log claim, work, submit, stop and release.  The coordinator also logs merges and send-backs.  Sessions record their role, their parent and the model.

The rule was that tracking must stay tiny and never slow the swarm down.  This is real data, trimmed: one worker, one issue, about 25 minutes from claim to submit.
:::

## What the timeline revealed

```{=html}
<div class="fn-timeline artifact">
  <div class="artifact-bar"><span>one lane per agent</span><span>time →</span></div>
  <div class="fn-lane"><b>coordinator</b><div><i class="w" style="left:2%;width:94%"></i><em class="m" style="left:30%"></em><em class="m" style="left:52%"></em><em class="m" style="left:88%"></em><em class="sb" style="left:70%"></em></div></div>
  <div class="fn-lane"><b>spruce</b><div><i class="w" style="left:6%;width:22%"></i><i class="w" style="left:34%;width:16%"></i><i class="dup" style="left:56%;width:12%"></i></div></div>
  <div class="fn-lane"><b>larch</b><div><i class="w" style="left:10%;width:18%"></i><i class="ab" style="left:40%;width:20%"></i><i class="w" style="left:66%;width:20%"></i></div></div>
  <div class="fn-lane"><b>rowan · mac</b><div><i class="w" style="left:20%;width:26%"></i><i class="sbk" style="left:50%;width:18%"></i></div></div>
  <div class="fn-lane dead"><b>alder</b><div><i class="w" style="left:4%;width:30%"></i><i class="dead" style="left:34%;width:40%"></i></div></div>
  <div class="fn-legend"><span><i class="w"></i>work</span><span><i class="dup"></i>duplicate</span><span><i class="ab"></i>abandoned</span><span><i class="sbk"></i>sent back</span><span><i class="dead"></i>dead session</span><span><em class="m"></em>merge</span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Swarm B turns those lines into a timeline, one lane per agent.  This is an illustration of what it shows, not a screenshot.

Seeing it laid out was humbling.  Two workers on the same issue.  Work that was abandoned partway.  Merge requests sent back.  And sessions that had quietly died while still holding a claim, which is why the inspector now tells dead lanes from waiting ones from active ones.
:::

## Waste is a metric

```{=html}
<div class="fn-waste">
  <div class="fn-w"><span class="eyebrow">DUPLICATE</span><b>Overlapping claims</b><small>the work each duplicate threw away, and a redundancy figure</small></div>
  <div class="fn-w"><span class="eyebrow">ABANDONED</span><b>Why each span ended</b><small>duplicate · released · blocked · sent back · dead agent</small></div>
  <div class="fn-w"><span class="eyebrow">SENT BACK</span><b>A state of its own</b><small>visible on the board while the worker is still in session</small></div>
  <div class="fn-w"><span class="eyebrow">STUCK</span><b>Dead, waiting, or active?</b><small>the coordinator can close a dead session's claim</small></div>
</div>
<p class="fn-caption">Credit goes to the merge that landed, not to the effort.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Once the waste was visible, it became something to measure and reduce.

Duplicate work shows up as overlapping claims, with the span each duplicate threw away and an overall redundancy figure.  Abandoned work is labelled with why it ended.  Sent-back work gets its own state on the board.  Stale lanes are classified as dead, waiting or active, and the coordinator can close a dead session.

And credit is strict: a released or abandoned stretch only gets credit for a merge if its own merge request is the one that landed.
:::

## Capacity is measured, not guessed

```{=html}
<div class="fn-capacity">
  <div class="fn-gauge">
    <div class="fn-gauge-n">3</div>
    <div class="fn-gauge-l">workers per swarm<br>on one desktop</div>
  </div>
  <div class="fn-cap-rules">
    <div><b>Ask first</b><span>each worker checks capacity before its full gate</span></div>
    <div><b>Zero means wait</b><span>or check only what changed</span></div>
    <div><b>Build vs read helpers</b><span>read helpers are never refused for build load; at most 4 per worker</span></div>
    <div><b>Heavy tests sparingly</b><span>slow tests once, twice to confirm; repeats belong in CI</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="fn-caption">The worker count came from measuring builds on the machine, not from a guess.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
It's tempting to keep adding workers.  On one desktop, builds and heavy tests compete for the same cores, memory and devices, and past a point you just slow everyone down.

So capacity became a command with a measured rule, not a guess.  Each worker asks it before running the full gate; if it says zero, the worker waits or runs only the checks for what changed.  Helper sub-agents are split into build helpers and read helpers: readers are cheap and never refused, but capped at four per worker.

The measured answer was three workers per swarm on my desktop.
:::

## Rules written in pain

```{=html}
<div class="fn-pain">
  <div><b>End what you launch</b><span>no test apps, windows or crash dialogs left behind</span></div>
  <div><b>Failures must be loud</b><span>I hit a silent failure; now the UI must say so</span></div>
  <div><b>Scrub what you spill</b><span>no user or host names in output files</span></div>
  <div><b>Clean up worktrees</b><span>and their build directories, when the issue closes</span></div>
  <div><b>Leave my checkout alone</b><span>it stays on main; agents work in worktrees</span></div>
  <div><b>No dead controls</b><span>a control that does nothing on a tab isn't shown there</span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Many of the directions are rules I only wrote after something went wrong.

Test runs left windows and crash dialogs all over the desktop, so every test now ends what it launched.  I hit a failure that the UI didn't report, so failures must be visible.  Output files contained user and host names, so they're scrubbed.  Worktrees and build directories piled up, so workers remove them when their issue closes.  An agent switched my own checkout off main, so agents work only in worktrees.  And controls that did nothing on some tabs got hidden there.
:::

## Risky code lives at named seams

```{=html}
<div class="fn-seams">
  <div class="fn-seam-core">
    <div class="eyebrow">DEFAULT</div>
    <b>Safe code everywhere</b>
    <span>unsafe denied across the workspace</span>
  </div>
  <div class="fn-seam-list">
    <div><b>Approved modules only</b><span>each exception named, planned, and signed off by the owner</span></div>
    <div><b>Every block justified</b><span>a SAFETY comment on each one; none in generated code</span></div>
    <div><b>Decisions stay safe</b><span>layout and ordering are decided in safe code above the seam</span></div>
    <div><b>Only our own processes</b><span>launch what we create; never touch a running one</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Some code has to do risky things: call native APIs, talk to the OS, launch other processes.  The rule was that unsafe code is denied everywhere by default, and each exception is a named module that I approve as part of a plan.

Inside those modules, every unsafe block carries a safety comment, and none appears in generated code.  The decisions, like memory layout and ordering, are made in safe code above the seam.  And the launcher only ever starts processes it creates; it never attaches to one that's already running.
:::

## Two swarms in step

```{=html}
<div class="fn-step2">
  <div class="fn-repo a"><b>Swarm A</b><span>the product</span></div>
  <div class="fn-mid">
    <div class="fn-contract">versioned tracking contract</div>
    <div class="fn-sync"><span>→ tracking format, nested sessions</span></div>
    <div class="fn-sync back"><span>← helpers, capacity rule, worker count</span></div>
    <div class="fn-mid-notes"><span>a twin sync issue for every shared change</span><span>a lint that catches drift</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="fn-repo b"><b>Swarm B</b><span>the inspector</span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Two swarms sharing a process will drift apart unless something holds them together.

The tracking format became a versioned contract.  Every shared change gets a twin sync issue in the other repository, and a lint checks for drift.

Improvements really did flow both ways.  The tracking format and nested sessions went from the product swarm to the inspector.  The helper rules, the measured capacity rule and the worker count were worked out in the inspector swarm, then pulled back into the product swarm a day later.
:::

## The owner's job

```{=html}
<div class="fn-owner">
  <div class="fn-quote">“Keep going without waiting for prompts.”</div>
  <div class="fn-quote">“Give headlines when batches land.”</div>
  <div class="fn-quote">“Keep going until it's a nice stable feature set.”</div>
  <div class="fn-quote">“Sweep every command and pane; fix; sweep again.”</div>
</div>
<div class="fn-owner-roles"><span>direction</span><span>approvals</span><span>quality bars</span><span>headlines, not transcripts</span></div>
```

::: {.notes}
These are real directions from the ledger, and together they describe the job.

The swarm runs autonomously.  I don't want to approve every step; I want headlines when a batch lands.  My part is direction, approving plans and risky changes, and setting the quality bar.

The quality bar matters most near the end.  "A nice stable feature set" turned into a stability sweep of every command and pane, the defects fixed, then a second sweep to confirm.
:::

## Start a new swarm from an old one

```{=html}
<div class="fn2-clone">
  <div class="fn2-box a"><div class="eyebrow">SWARM A</div><b>A working swarm</b><span>a week of hard-won process</span></div>
  <div class="fn2-carry">
    <div class="eyebrow">COPIED ACROSS</div>
    <div class="fn-chips"><span>AGENTS.md</span><span>architecture</span><span>command layer</span><span>UI shell</span><span>control channel</span><span>agent tools</span><span>claim → merge process</span><span>labels</span><span>templates</span><span>CI layout</span></div>
    <div class="fn2-left">Left behind: the old product's domain code</div>
  </div>
  <div class="fn2-box b"><div class="eyebrow">SWARM B</div><b>A clean starter</b><span>~420 commits in its first three days</span></div>
</div>
<p class="fn-caption">The second swarm started fast because its process came ready-made.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Swarm B didn't start from nothing.  It started from a clean copy of Swarm A's guidance and architecture: the AGENTS.md, the command layer, the UI shell, the control channel and agent tools, and the whole claim-to-merge process.  Its project even got the same labels, templates and CI layout.

What it left behind was Swarm A's domain code.  The new product only needed the scaffolding.

The result was a swarm that was productive within hours, because none of the process had to be rediscovered.
:::

## Set the pace, and stage per feature

```{=html}
<div class="fn2-pace">
  <div class="fn2-targets">
    <div class="eyebrow">THE OWNER'S PACE TARGETS</div>
    <div class="fn2-target"><b>12 h</b><span>first major feature working</span></div>
    <div class="fn2-target"><b>18 h</b><span>the second feature</span></div>
    <div class="fn2-days"><span><b>Day 2</b> alpha</span><span><b>Day 3</b> beta for the first feature</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="fn2-stages">
    <div class="eyebrow">STAGES ARE PER FEATURE</div>
    <div class="fn2-stage"><span>Feature 1</span><i class="beta">beta</i></div>
    <div class="fn2-stage"><span>Feature 2</span><i class="alpha">alpha</i></div>
    <div class="fn2-stage"><span>Feature 3</span><i class="pre">pre-alpha</i></div>
    <div class="fn2-stage"><span>Feature 4</span><i class="pre">pre-alpha</i></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
I gave the swarm explicit pace targets: the first major feature working within 12 hours, and the second within 18.  They were ambitious, and having a number changed how the work was planned.

The project went alpha on its second day, and the first feature reached beta the day after.  But a single stage for the whole product stopped making sense quickly.  Stages are tracked per feature instead, so one part can be beta while another is still pre-alpha, and everyone, agents included, knows how much to trust each one.
:::

## Real data from the first milestone

```{=html}
<div class="fn-vs">
  <div class="fn-card bad">
    <div class="eyebrow">TEMPTING</div>
    <b>Fixtures only</b>
    <ul>
      <li>Hand-made sample data</li>
      <li>Always tidy, always small</li>
      <li>Looks finished in a demo</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
  <div class="fn-vs-mark">→</div>
  <div class="fn-card good">
    <div class="eyebrow">THE FIRST MILESTONE</div>
    <b>The real swarm, live</b>
    <ul>
      <li>One lane per real agent</li>
      <li>Refreshed as it works</li>
      <li>Tests keep data of their own</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="fn-caption">The same lesson as toy targets, applied from the very start.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
For Swarm B, the first milestone wasn't allowed to be a demo on made-up data.  It had to show Swarm A's real tracking data, one lane per agent, refreshed live.

That's the toy-target lesson applied up front.  Real data is messy, large and surprising, and it found problems that fixtures never would.  Tests still use repositories of their own, so they stay repeatable.
:::

## Two machines, one swarm

```{=html}
<div class="fn2-machines">
  <div class="fn2-machine"><b>Desktop</b><span>workers + coordinator</span><span>the heavy tests</span></div>
  <div class="fn2-hub"><div class="eyebrow">THE TRACKER</div><b>Live claims</b><span>labels and comments, not files in the repo</span></div>
  <div class="fn2-machine mac"><b>Mac</b><span>workers of its own</span><span>claims like everyone else</span></div>
</div>
<p class="fn-caption">The coordinator merges the Mac's work as it's ready, like any other worker's.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Both swarms ran on more than one machine: a desktop doing the heavy lifting, and a Mac taking work too.

The Mac's workers claim issues exactly like the desktop's, and the coordinator merges their merge requests as they're ready.  This is the real reason the issue tracker stayed the board.  A checked-in Kanban folder can't give two machines a shared, live view of who has claimed what.
:::

## Keep the record honest

```{=html}
<div class="fn2-honest">
  <div class="artifact fn-jsonl">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>fix history, and mark it</span><span>retro</span></div>
<pre><code>{"event":"claim","issue":12}
{"event":"work","issue":12,"retro":true}
{"event":"submit","issue":12}</code></pre>
    <p class="fn2-note">When the tracking rules changed, old data was amended to match, and every amended line says so.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="fn2-infer">
    <div class="eyebrow">INFER WHAT WASN'T LOGGED</div>
    <div class="fn2-mini"><i class="claim">claim</i><i class="gap">inferred work</i><i class="submit">submit</i></div>
    <p class="fn2-note">A claim, then a submit, with no work logged between: the gap is drawn as work, but dimmer.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Tracking data is only useful if it's honest about its own gaps.

When the tracking rules changed, the swarm went back and amended its old data to the new rules.  Every amended line is marked retro, so nobody mistakes a reconstruction for a live record.

And when an agent claimed an issue and later submitted it without logging any work in between, the inspector infers that work happened, but draws it dimmer.  It fills the gap, and still shows that it's a guess.
:::

## Measure the agents, not just the code

```{=html}
<div class="fn2-insights">
  <div><b>Where the time goes</b><span>across agents and issues</span></div>
  <div><b>Pipelines</b><span>merge requests in CI</span></div>
  <div><b>Alerts</b><span>when something needs attention</span></div>
  <div><b>Time-lapse</b><span>watch the work unfold</span></div>
  <div class="hi"><b>Compare</b><span>agents, roles and models</span></div>
  <div><b>Daily report</b><span>a summary of each day</span></div>
</div>
<p class="fn-caption">Each session now records its model, so models can be compared on real work.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Once the swarm was visible, the next question was how well it works, not just what it built.  These are the ideas on the inspector's backlog: where the time goes, merge-request pipelines, alerts, a time-lapse of the work, comparisons between agents, roles and models, and a daily report.

The comparison needed one small change in the product swarm too: every session now records which model it ran.  That turns "which model is better for this?" into something you can measure on real work.
:::

## Directions change, and that's fine

```{=html}
<div class="stage document-stage">
  <div class="artifact paper fn-ledger">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>revision history</span><span>newest first</span></div>
    <div class="fn-line"><i>10-19</i><span>Three workers per swarm; gates wait for capacity</span></div>
    <div class="fn-line"><i>10-19</i><span>Helpers in worktrees; capacity measured</span></div>
    <div class="fn-line"><i>10-17</i><span>Every agent logs to the tracking branch</span></div>
    <div class="fn-line"><i>10-16</i><span>Progress in the MR; summaries per batch</span></div>
    <div class="fn-line"><i>10-15</i><span>The UI must report failures</span></div>
    <div class="fn-line"><i>10-15</i><span>First version: the owner's notes, folded in</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="side-copy">
    <p class="big-claim compact">The ledger records direction as given, not as it should have been.</p>
    <p>I changed my mind about layering, focus and process along the way.</p>
    <p class="accent-note">A dated history beats a perfect plan.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
I didn't get the direction right first time.  I updated the layering guidance, moved the focus off the toy target, and changed the process several times as problems showed up.

The ledger doesn't hide that.  It records directions as I gave them, with dates, and a revision table shows how they changed.  That's more useful than pretending there was a perfect plan, because a new worker can see both the current rule and why it exists.

The revision rows here are paraphrased from Swarm A's ledger, with their real dates.
:::

## Environment traps

```{=html}
<div class="fn2-trap">
  <div class="fn2-chain">
    <div><i>1</i><span>Launched as administrator</span></div>
    <div><i>2</i><span>The app it started ran as administrator too</span></div>
    <div><i>3</i><span>That app ignored our environment settings</span></div>
    <div class="bad"><i>4</i><span>Nothing connected, and nothing said why</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="fn2-fix">
    <div class="eyebrow">THE FIXES</div>
    <div class="fn-hop"><b>Launch with normal rights</b><span>as the original product does</span></div>
    <div class="fn-hop"><b>Make failure loud</b><span>a target that crashes, exits or never connects must say so</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Not every failure is in the code.  One of mine was the environment.

Run as administrator, the tool launched its target as administrator too.  An elevated process ignored the environment settings the tool relied on, so nothing ever connected, and nothing told me why.

The fixes were to launch targets with normal rights, as the original product does, and to make the UI report any target that crashes, exits or never connects.  That second rule is in the ledger because of this.
:::

## Small decisions that paid off

```{=html}
<div class="fn-pain">
  <div><b>Web from day one</b><span>keep the core browser-clean from the start</span></div>
  <div><b>Borrow performance targets</b><span>take the numbers that transfer from the original's own code</span></div>
  <div><b>Borrow the look and feel</b><span>familiar to the original's users; small accessibility fixes kept for review</span></div>
  <div><b>Defer on purpose</b><span>code signing and CI runners waited, and the ledger says so</span></div>
  <div><b>Ask the original's owners</b><span>an open question becomes a ticket for them, not a guess</span></div>
  <div><b>Merge on the local gate</b><span>don't wait for CI; stop merging while main is red</span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
A handful of smaller calls that turned out well.

Swarm B kept its core clean enough to build for the browser from day one.  Performance targets that made sense were copied from the original product's code, rather than invented.  The look and feel follows the original, so its users feel at home, with a few accessibility fixes kept aside for review.

Some things were deferred deliberately, like code signing and CI runners, and the ledger records that, so nobody wastes time on them.  Where the original's behaviour was unclear, the swarm filed a question for the original's owners rather than guessing.  And merges happen on a green local gate rather than waiting for the CI queue, with merging paused whenever main goes red.
:::

## Field notes, in one slide {.final-slide}

```{=html}
<div class="recipe">
  <div><i>01</i><b>Keep a dated ledger</b><span>Every owner decision, one line, newest wins.</span></div>
  <div><i>02</i><b>Copy something real</b><span>A golden reference and an oracle beat a spec.</span></div>
  <div><i>03</i><b>Test on real workloads</b><span>Toy targets bend the code around them.</span></div>
  <div><i>04</i><b>Keep shared files cold</b><span>Progress in the MR; summaries per batch.</span></div>
  <div><i>05</i><b>Log every claim</b><span>A tiny event stream makes the swarm visible.</span></div>
  <div><i>06</i><b>Measure the waste</b><span>Duplicate, abandoned and sent-back work.</span></div>
  <div><i>07</i><b>Measure capacity</b><span>More workers is not more progress.</span></div>
  <div><i>08</i><b>Answer questions</b><span>The owner decides; the swarm plans and builds.</span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
If I had to keep only eight lessons, these are them.
:::
